issue.title: mindspore.dataset.transforms.vision.c_transforms 必须和dataset.map搭配使用吗？

body:
1. 在python端无法直接调用vision.c_transforms（c++实现）下的数据增强算子来处理Tensor
2. 但是，mindspore.dataset还提供另外一套数据增强算子vision.py_transforms（python实现），且处理的类型是numpy array，因此需要将Tensor转成成numpy array类型（Tensor.asnumpy()）之后进行使用，使用举例：

```
import mindspore.dataset.transforms.vision.py_transforms as py_vision
import numpy as np
import mindspore.common.dtype as mstype
from mindspore import Tensor

input_tensor = Tensor(np.random.rand(24, 12, 3), mstype.float32)
hwc2chw = py_vision.HWC2CHW()
output = hwc2chw(input_tensor.asnumpy())
output_tensor = Tensor(output)
```

body:
The related PR from Linh: https://gitee.com/mindspore/mindspore/pulls/121

Hi, Linh. Thank you for your RFC & PR. It is a good step to do type-preserved opt to reduce the cost of renorm. 

I have two question.
Question 1: Can renorm of opt_a also be checked? As in the last iteration of opt_a, the renorm may be reduntant.

Quetions 2: I think there maybe unsufficient that whether there is a case the new substituted result node is typed while some of its inputs are constructed with untyped? If there is no such case in our current opt_b passes currently, we need to add this as a new rule to all passes. If there are some untyped nodes in substituted nodes, the root of these nodes must be untyped. 
There may be three choices we can choose to make sure all the sub-passes are "shallow".
Choice 1 is obey the rule manually. Every new subtree to replace has to obey the rule "if ever a subnode is untyped then the root must be untyped". 
Choice 2 is to use "local type inference". Because before substitution every happens, type information is complete and thus all the types of the parameter are there; so every subnode in the subtree that is parameter can be easily typed -- in that way an easy bottom up, linear time inference is possible. But, if there is a global level renorm behind the current pass, the local level type infer is reduntant.
Choice 3 is to refact our IR interface to have a single "standardized" method of graph modifying in our infrastructure, like LLVM replaceAllUsesWith. So that, we can make sure all the new nodes are typed or untyped.
I think we can combine Choice 1 and Choice 3 to add a check when we relace the nodes. By using the nodes() or all_nodes() from graph manager, we can travel all the new nodes from the root node easyly.

> Hi, Linh. Thank you for your RFC & PR. It is a good step to do type-preserved opt to reduce the cost of renorm. 
> 
> I have two question.
> Question 1: Can renorm of opt_a also be checked? As in the last iteration of opt_a, the renorm may be reduntant.
> 
> Quetions 2: I think there maybe unsufficient that whether there is a case the new substituted result node is typed while some of its inputs are constructed with untyped? If there is no such case in our current opt_b passes currently, we need to add this as a new rule to all passes. If there are some untyped nodes in substituted nodes, the root of these nodes must be untyped. 
> There may be three choices we can choose to make sure all the sub-passes are "shallow".
> Choice 1 is obey the rule manually. Every new subtree to replace has to obey the rule "if ever a subnode is untyped then the root must be untyped". 
> Choice 2 is to use "local type inference". Because before substitution every happens, type information is complete and thus all the types of the parameter are there; so every subnode in the subtree that is parameter can be easily typed -- in that way an easy bottom up, linear time inference is possible. But, if there is a global level renorm behind the current pass, the local level type infer is reduntant.
> Choice 3 is to refact our IR interface to have a single "standardized" method of graph modifying in our infrastructure, like LLVM replaceAllUsesWith. So that, we can make sure all the new nodes are typed or untyped.
> I think we can combine Choice 1 and Choice 3 to add a check when we relace the nodes. By using the nodes() or all_nodes() from graph manager, we can travel all the new nodes from the root node easyly. 

@kungsen  I actually don't quite understand your concerns on "redundant computation" in Choice 2 because in my opinion, Choice 1 and Choice 2 should be the same linear complexity (traversal of the subtree). The only reason I think Choice 1 should be preferred is its simplicity in implementation; but Choice 2 makes more sense because its logic is more direct compared to Choice 1. (we are facing problems of untyped nodes).
I think the "redundancy" only appears in the sense of code duplication.

issue.title: "Typed"-Tag Indicating well-typedness of a whole subtree for Type Preserving

body:
> Hi, Ende.
> Thank you for your idea. It is interesting because it gives a new view to see the problem.
> I think the proposed Typed<> likes a special monad with the semantic "all the subtree in a Typed<AnfNode> are Typed<>". With this semantic, we can be confidential to do renorm or not after a transform pass.
> According to your intro, I have several questions.
> Question1: How can "Typed" tag make sure its subtree are all typed?
> Question2: When and where can we change untyped node to typed node? I think it should be ProgramSpecializer.
> Question3: Can untyped node replace typed node? For example "SimplifyDataStructures". Or only typed node can be replaced?
> Question4: I think we can get all new nodes from manager. If we use manager to track all new nodes, do we still need Typed<>?
> Question5: Why prefer co-variant template to achive "Typed" tag?

@kungsen  Thanks Gongchen for these questions.
Answer 1: it is ensured by the restriction of the constructor of each `Typed<..>`, you can see from above how  I define the constructor of `Typed<..>`. Basically by induction, if base case (ValueNode/ParameterNode) are typed and inductive case (ApplyNode) are typed, then the whole subtree is typed.

Answer 2: `Typed<>` tag is not to replace `x->abstract()`, it is more of a convenient/compile-time and tun-time showing indication for a subtree of typed node, so that later a pass, if its precondition is all typed nodes, then it doesn't have to spend linear time to statically check everything, but just at type-declaration put `Typed<AnfNode>` as input parameter. 
Also, It is an infrastructure to help the developer (and maybe compiler can get away with duplicated computation) instead of really helping the compiler to generate better code. So at anytime if every node in a subtree is typed, then the developer can easily transform it (by linear time) into a typed tree by tagging each node into `Typed<AnfNode>`, and later any addition of new untyped node must be the parent of some `Typed<>` Node (due to the restriction of the constructor of `Typed<>` Node), then partial renormalization can certainly know that range to partial renormalize

Answer 3. For In-place mutation, only typed-node can replace typed-node. If you want to have untyped-node to replace typed node, then one of the following must be satisfied:
- make the untyped node typed (but setting `->abstract`)
- use recursive style/immutable style IRMutator/IRFunctor so that when replacing with an untyped node, all the parents of the untyped node will change to untyped
- The point is we maintain an invariant -- there can never be an typed node has a child as untyped

Question 4: Can I just use an auxiliary data structure that stores all the untyped nodes in the current manager?
- You will have a lot of trouble doing that, with your own example, because you break the invariance above. Consider the following situation -- you have a tree structure  untyped node <- a typed node 'X' <- newly replacing untyped 'Y' <- typed Tree. With the new untyped node 'Y' in the middle, the once typed node 'X' is actually untyped because its type is incorrect (except for the trivial case the untyped 'Y' doesn't change its type, in that case you already know the type and can directly put a type on `Y` then insert). While `X` is not in your global-state data structure - 'new-nodes' queue of the manager. 
You may ask Question: we can maintain some sorts of invariance on the data structure in graph manager?
- That's exactly what I did here. I maintain this invariance by restricting the constructor. `Typed<>` is provably correct because of the restriction on its constructor (I have shown you the induction). While a simple data structure in you graph manager is not, and also to maintain that data structure you might end up adding the code with same logic (to check the invariance) everywhere.
- Also I prefer `Typed<>` because it gives a compile-time static checking/specification. (If a pass/program transformation wants typed nodes, then it just needs to say the input parameter is of `Typed<AnfNode>`). You cannot do the same with just a simple "track all new nodes"
- And the information is directly attach to the nodes instead of the global-monster manager
- `Typed<>` also gives possibility to IRBuilder.

Answer 5:
Because currently `Typed<X>` is just a subclass of X; but consider `Typed<Parameter>` is a subclass of `Typed<AnfNode>`, which means `Typed<>` should be a covariant w.r.t. the sub-classing relationship.


And I am sorry I cannot see it as a Monad. I can see it as a functor in a category where objects are typed and arrows are subclassing relations.

> @thlinh As you modified the checking action, could you please update the results of the different networks mentioned in this issue? And I prefer the total time should be added to the results. You can get it easily in the log.

@biffex : I have re-run the tests with MS master repo (before PR) and with changes in PR. Here are the latest results (run on my blue laptop). In general the checking takes some amount of time, but the total performance is still improved about 70% for the renormalize passes.
 
- For BERT: Originally the opt_b.renormalize takes about 2.93% of the total (parsing) time, opt_control.renormalize takes 1.47%, which contributes a total of 4.5%. With the changes in this RRC, the total time drop to almost 1.64%.
![输入图片说明](https://images.gitee.com/uploads/images/2020/0410/002653_1cb46fb3_6571702.png "Screenshot from 2020-04-09 12-25-46.png")
- For RESNET train test: Originally the total time for opt_b and opt_control passes uses 5,4% of total time, with this RFC, the total time drops to 1,99%.
![输入图片说明](https://images.gitee.com/uploads/images/2020/0410/002452_0b117755_6571702.png "Screenshot from 2020-04-09 12-23-27.png")
- For RESNET infer test: Originally the time for opt_b (no opt_control in this case) was 0,67%. With this RFC, the time drops to almost 0%.
![输入图片说明](https://images.gitee.com/uploads/images/2020/0410/002301_05ce1772_6571702.png "Screenshot from 2020-04-09 12-22-03.png")
- For LeNet network: Originally the time for opt_b and opt_control passes was 3,64%. With this RFC, the time again drops to 1.25%.
![输入图片说明](https://images.gitee.com/uploads/images/2020/0410/001322_f92037f3_6571702.png "屏幕截图.png")

body: @kungsen : There is cases (for example in `test_graph_return_const_param.py`), where the `"return"` was single node of type AbstractTensor (no other nodes were generated) but still need a full Renormalize to be well-typed. And there are obviously (as can be seen in validator.cc) types that are not supported later (at back-end), which will cause the validating agent to raise Exception there. So for those types, I still set to call the Renormalize to: 1. have the node further processed, 2. there may be a chance that a part of Renormalize (like Specialize) can deal with those nodes with unsupport types so that it would pass the validating later. By adding more cases for "2", we sacrifice a little in the performance with the hope that we can support better more cases, but it will be safer for the parser.

> @kungsen  Thanks Gongchen for these questions.
> Answer 1: it is ensured by the restriction of the constructor of each `Typed<..>`, you can see from above how  I define the constructor of `Typed<..>`. Basically by induction, if base case (ValueNode/ParameterNode) are typed and inductive case (ApplyNode) are typed, then the whole subtree is typed.
> Answer 2: `Typed<>` tag is not to replace `x->abstract()`, it is more of a convenient/compile-time and tun-time showing indication for a subtree of typed node, so that later a pass, if its precondition is all typed nodes, then it doesn't have to spend linear time to statically check everything, but just at type-declaration put `Typed<AnfNode>` as input parameter. 
> Also, It is an infrastructure to help the developer (and maybe compiler can get away with duplicated computation) instead of really helping the compiler to generate better code. So at anytime if every node in a subtree is typed, then the developer can easily transform it (by linear time) into a typed tree by tagging each node into `Typed<AnfNode>`, and later any addition of new untyped node must be the parent of some `Typed<>` Node (due to the restriction of the constructor of `Typed<>` Node), then partial renormalization can certainly know that range to partial renormalize
> Answer 3. For In-place mutation, only typed-node can replace typed-node. If you want to have untyped-node to replace typed node, then one of the following must be satisfied:
> - make the untyped node typed (but setting `->abstract`)
> - use recursive style/immutable style IRMutator/IRFunctor so that when replacing with an untyped node, all the parents of the untyped node will change to untyped
> - The point is we maintain an invariant -- there can never be an typed node has a child as untyped
> Question 4: Can I just use an auxiliary data structure that stores all the untyped nodes in the current manager?
> - You will have a lot of trouble doing that, with your own example, because you break the invariance above. Consider the following situation -- you have a tree structure  untyped node <- a typed node 'X' <- newly replacing untyped 'Y' <- typed Tree. With the new untyped node 'Y' in the middle, the once typed node 'X' is actually untyped because its type is incorrect (except for the trivial case the untyped 'Y' doesn't change its type, in that case you already know the type and can directly put a type on `Y` then insert). While `X` is not in your global-state data structure - 'new-nodes' queue of the manager. 
> You may ask Question: we can maintain some sorts of invariance on the data structure in graph manager?
> - That's exactly what I did here. I maintain this invariance by restricting the constructor. `Typed<>` is provably correct because of the restriction on its constructor (I have shown you the induction). While a simple data structure in you graph manager is not, and also to maintain that data structure you might end up adding the code with same logic (to check the invariance) everywhere.
> - Also I prefer `Typed<>` because it gives a compile-time static checking/specification. (If a pass/program transformation wants typed nodes, then it just needs to say the input parameter is of `Typed<AnfNode>`). You cannot do the same with just a simple "track all new nodes"
> - And the information is directly attach to the nodes instead of the global-monster manager
> - `Typed<>` also gives possibility to IRBuilder.
> Answer 5:
> Because currently `Typed<X>` is just a subclass of X; but consider `Typed<Parameter>` is a subclass of `Typed<AnfNode>`, which means `Typed<>` should be a covariant w.r.t. the sub-classing relationship.
> And I am sorry I cannot see it as a Monad. I can see it as a functor in a category where objects are typed and arrows are subclassing relations.

@endejin  Thank you for your detailed explaination. I am still uncertain if this suit for our IR system. For example, "use recursive style/immutable style IRMutator/IRFunctor so that when replacing with an untyped node, all the parents of the untyped node will change to untyped", this may be unacceptable for AD and AutoParallel transformation.

issue.title: Bugs in the Abstract Interpreter (AI) based Inference Engine

body:
The test-cases all seem simple and don't look like corner cases. Apart from that, there are some comments here.
* __Not Clear Specification__ : Related to tuples, sometimes it can be compiled, sometimes it cannot be compiled. The user will be totally confused.
* __Require Explicit Halting by decreasing argument__ : Currently a simple unhalting while-loop can easily make compiler unhalt and exit with segementation fault. Let alone the fact that unhalting program might end up useful when side effect are introduced, a compiler should not attempt to [solve halting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halting_problem). 
* __Fixpoint is still required__ : Facing the lack of fixpoint, an attempt removing subtyping relation between `Int` and `Float` is made but is not enough. Since we have tuples : `(Int32, Int32, kMetaTypeAnything) <: (Int32, kMetaTypeAnything, kMetaTypeAnything) <: (kMetaTypeAnything, kMetaTypeAnything, kMetaTypeAnything)`, which can still lead to an extremely high lattice. The tuple-transpose example is a natural example to reflect this deficiency.
* __Addition may lose type precesion__ : Currently addition of int32 and float32 will lead to `AbstractScalar(kMetaTypeAnything)`, which is essentially a float32 because you don't know anything but consider it as a scalar and thus you will lean on the most conservative choice. 
    * Adding type-casting operation (from int32 to float32) is essentially **a poorman's version of type annotation** which isn't endorsed. (Their original word: "Type annotations makes it like writing C++ code") 
    * Currently this adhoc lifiting is okay, but when the type `UInt32` and `Int32` or `Int16` added together, lifting to `MetaTypeAnything` is bad because the type information as Integer may later be used as a guard to do `getitem` indexing on tuples. **For example when runtime value as indexing on `List` (which should be supported in the future)**. In other words, `[1,2,3][(int32) 1 + (uint32) 1]` won't be supported, because the inner type is `kMetaTypeAnything`. This will reject more program.
    * You still need to have a distinction between Int and Float, and consider "int + float would lead to float; int + uint would lead to int" to do Type Promotion correctly when type-checking. 

* I also think Tagged/Untagged Union is a very important feature; as part of the algebraic data type, with that you can encode `List`, which is **exactly how Myia does that**. Without Tagged/Untagged Union, in the future, a lot of features will be extended in an ad-hoc way. 

We know that if fixpoint is introduced, then all the error will be resolved, because the fixpoint is something that **HAS ACADEMIC PAPER SUPPORTING IT**.  However, there is risk to slow down the infer when fixpoint is properly introduced. It is basically a dilemma.

issue.title: summary写入模块优化备忘录

body:
很细致的工作，为你点赞！

个人的一些评论如下：

## 修改方案1

修改方案1 `从“串行 - 并行处理（无锁） - 并行写入（有锁）”改成“串行 - 并行处理 - 串行写入”。` 

如果这个方案只能处理step乱序的问题，那建议暂缓实施，MindInsight已经兼容了step乱序的情况。此外，如果这个方案降低了性能，那应该重新审视这个方案。


## 修改方案2

`数据进入缓存时，从现在追加数据的方式改为直接覆盖原有数据。`  覆盖规则是什么？ 建议使用 `覆盖相同(tag, 插件类型eg scalar， image)下的原有数据`。

## 修改方案4

如果要删除写入Summary文件的字段，请提前和测试沟通。 max， min字段不要删除。


## 其它建议1

`flush_step词不达意容易误导，建议改成record_step.` 或者改为 record_interval ?

## 其它建议2

`CRC32校验或许不是必要的`

这里是参考了TensorFlow的设计，加入了CRC32校验的机制。而Tensorflow的summary文件实际上是TFRecord的格式，TFRecord作为TensorFlow的通用数据存储格式，设置CRC32以识别文件内容是否出现错误，我觉得是合理的。

当然，我们的summary文件是否需要CRC32可以再讨论。

## 其它建议3

`TensorProto的实现目前存在缺陷` -- 存在什么缺陷？


## 其它建议5

`SummaryStep` 应该考虑提供context_manager

## 其它建议8

`action to reaction` 什么意思？

## 其它建议10

`目前直方图的binning可能存在step与step之间不对齐的问题。`为了降低mindspore summary代码的复杂度，没有在mindspore summary代码中记录同一tag的直方图的跨step的范围情况。由于mindspore summary每隔flush_step就会写入文件，很难再去调整已写入数据的binning。 step和step不对齐的问题是mindinsight解决的。

body:
Hi All, recently I worked on the poc in this [branch](https://gitee.com/zichun_ye/mindspore/tree/type_tag_poc/). In the poc, I worked on the following items

1. create the classes with typed tag for `AnfNode`, `CNode`, and `Parameter` and the cast function between them;
2. `underlyingnode` and `underlyingtree` methods that link the tagged class back to the untagged ones;
3. `set_typed_tag` function that set tags for the untagged node.

Here are some key points in the design:
1. For `cnode`, we rewrite the `set_input` and `set_inputs` as a virtual function. When the `set_input` and `set_inputs` are called in a typed node, they will check the `abstract` and return error if `abstract` is null.
2. `underlyingnode` and `underlyingtree` returns the node itself for `Parameter`, but create a new node for `cnode`
3. `set_typed_tag` set tags for the nodes inside one func_graph to avoid recursive issue.

Still there are some problems in this poc:
1. `set_typed_tag` create a new node with the same information. This would lead to an issue of the compiling time. Also, we are not sure whether it would lead an issue whether the new typed parameter node is the same as the old untyped one or not. For this problem, we tried to solve it by adding the typed tag to the pointer instead of the class object, but it is hard to overloading functions such as `set_input` and `set_inputs`.
2. `set_typed_tag` set tags for the nodes inside one func_graph. We need further a function to set tags for all graph. It would need the cooperation of the resource.

Also, we consider the usage of this typed class. The direct use of this class is in the ir mutator. However, ir mutator is under construction now, so maybe the best strategy is to keep this poc for now and wait until our first ir mutator comes into use so that we can update our design accordingly.

> And for Complexity, as we use shallow lattice (only one middle layer in most case), we using trace-based control flow analysis, instead of traditional fix-point. As a result, the complexity is also O(n), n can be see as the number of monomorphic nodes.

Hi @gongchen123 , it is not reasonable to say something about "Linear to the number of monomorphic nodes". Because the input of the compiler is the source code size, the users will not input monomorphic node. It only makes sense to say "Linear to the size of source code", which is exactly what we are emphasizing.
What's more, "linear to monomorphic node" is impling exponential (pseudo-polynomial) to the size of source code. Because we can have f : Shape[n] -> Shape[n] that will use f(Shape[n-1]).

class ParallelFcHyBridNet(Cell):
    def __init__(self, test_size, transpose_a=False, transpose_b=False, strategy=None, layerwise_parallel=True):
        super().__init__()
        weight_np = np.full(test_size, 0.1, dtype=np.float32)
        self.weight = Parameter(Tensor(weight_np), name="fc_weight", layerwise_parallel=layerwise_parallel)
        self.relu = ReLU()
        self.allgather = AllGather()
        self.fc = P.MatMul(transpose_a=transpose_a, transpose_b=transpose_b)
        self.fc.set_strategy(strategy)
        self.layerwise_parallel = layerwise_parallel

    def construct(self, inputs, label):
        x = self.relu(inputs)
        if self.layerwise_parallel:
            x = self.allgather(x)
        x = self.fc(x, self.weight)
        return x

> Great, Thanks @gongchen123 123 for your suggestion. Would you mind give us a concrete example for "polymorphic free variable"? We are really interested and looking forward to those non-usual test-cases. Thanks! 

@endejin  For a case of "polymorphic free var".
```
def test_make_tuple():
    # Staticly recursively creating static type is valid in mindspore.
    @ms_function
    def make_tuple(x):
        out = ()
        for i in range(3):
            out = out + (x,)
        return out
    res = make_tuple(5)
    assert res == (5, 5, 5)
```

![poly free var](https://images.gitee.com/uploads/images/2020/0510/071606_bc9b4b79_6568217.png "屏幕截图.png")

In the IR, `out` is a polymorphic free variable for the loop body. In out SA, we use context to find which evaluated out should be referened. HM has no context, so it means HM may has no support for the poly free var.

body:
> Another question, how can HM achieve the function of MetaFunction? Such as multitype operation(change + -> TensorAdd/ScalarAdd), do-signature, grad, hypermap?

@gongchen123 Hi Gongchen. As I have said, your "multitype operation" is essentially function overloading/adhoc polymorphism in the context of type inference. We have decided to adopt the classical solution from PL area instead of creating a solution ourselves -- using typeclass (in Haskell, also named as trait in Rust). The RFC of this part will be revealed soon.
Grad is not a problem since we can do "renormalization" as well again and the advantage for us is our HM is really linear to the size of the source code compared to AI-based (your trace-based), so even renormalization happens, it is empirically faster. I still hope someone can devote themselves into type-preserving gradient operation.

I don't know what do you mean by do-signature (the haskell's do?) and hypermap. If you can directly use standard terminology in Programming Language area, we can try to investigate the adoption of them with HM type system. Meanwhile, I am not too worried about that adoption will fail because we are essentially making wheels and consulting the other programming languages is the correct way to do. I also believe they have encountered the same problems and provided maybe even more mature solution.

body:
Perhaps you did not fully understand the dynamic programming algorithm. This may due to the writing of the paper. In any dynamic programming algorithm, some intermediate data should be stored. 

In this context, the final decisions (strategies of all operators) are made after considerring all operators. If the decision is made locally justing after looking at its own and its neighbor strategy, gobal optimum will be missed (and this is local search instead of dynamic programming).

Some writings of this paper may be confusing, but the iead is clear. I hope this can clarify your queries. 

In the aspect of runnig time of the current implemetation, the time for searching strategies for Resnet50 on 8 devices is less than 1 second, and the time for searching strategies on 64 devices is around 5 seconds. We think this is acceptable.

Thanks for posting this, and let us know if you have any further question.

Xiaoda

def test_distributed_sampler():

    sampler = DistributedSampler(64, 0, 8, shuffle=False)
    ds1 = ds.GeneratorDataset(source, ["data"], sampler=sampler)

    print("dataset size:", ds1.get_dataset_size())
    for data in ds1.create_dict_iterator():  # each data is a dictionary
        pass
```
The distributed Sampler in this case is a user customized one.
Our built in Distributed Sampler would also work
```
class DistributedSampler():

    def __init__(self, dataset_len, rank, group_size, shuffle=True, seed=0):
        self.rank = rank
        self.group_size = group_size
        self.dataset_length = dataset_len
        self.num_samples = int(math.ceil(self.dataset_length * 1.0 / self.group_size))
        self.total_size = self.num_samples * self.group_size
        self.shuffle = shuffle
        self.seed = seed

    def __iter__(self):
        if self.shuffle:
            self.seed = (self.seed + 1) & 0xffffffff
            np.random.seed(self.seed)
            indices = np.random.permutation(self.dataset_length).tolist()
        else:
            indices = list(range(self.dataset_length))

        indices += indices[:(self.total_size - len(indices))]
        indices = indices[self.rank::self.group_size]
        return iter(indices)

    def __len__(self):
        return self.num_samples
```
